topics.title: Threats to Data, Information, and Systems

subtopics.title: Types of External Threats to Data

items.definition: Malicious software designed to damage systems, steal data or gain unauthorised access.
items.examples: Ransomware locking hospital records; spyware logging banking passwords.
items.examTip: Describe how the specific type works, not just "malware".
keyFacts: Virus: attaches to files and spreads when they are run, so sharing one infected file can infect many PCs
Worm: spreads across networks by itself, so it can infect a whole organisation without anyone opening a file
Ransomware: encrypts files and demands payment, so the organisation cannot work until files are restored
Spyware: secretly records activity such as keystrokes, so passwords and bank details can be stolen
Trojan: disguised as legitimate software, so users install it themselves and let the attacker in

comparisonTable.title: Types of Malware Compared
rows: Attached to files; spreads when files shared/opened
Corrupts or deletes files; can spread across systems
Needs a host file; requires user to run it
No host file needed; spreads without user action
Email attachments, malicious downloads, exploit kits
Encrypts files; demands payment for decryption key
Victim's own data used as leverage
Bundled with free software; drive-by downloads
Records keystrokes, screenshots, browsing; steals credentials
Creates backdoor; installs other malware; steals data
Tricks user into installing it voluntarily
Bundled with free software or browser extensions
Displays unwanted ads; may track browsing
Often technically 'legal' if buried in terms

items.definition: Gaining access to a system or network without permission, e.g. by exploiting weaknesses or stolen passwords.
items.examples: Exploiting an unpatched web server to steal customer data.
items.examTip: Use the term "unauthorised access". Black-hat = malicious, white-hat = authorised testing.
keyFacts: Unpatched software is a key target, because attackers use known flaws that updates would have fixed
Brute force tries every password combination, so short, simple passwords are cracked quickly
Credential stuffing reuses leaked passwords, so one breach can unlock a person's other accounts
Motives include money, data theft and disruption, which is why valuable or high-profile targets are hit most

items.definition: Unintentional harm to hardware, software or data through human error or physical accidents.
items.examples: Deleting a database by mistake; spilling a drink on a server.
items.examTip: Separate accidental threats from deliberate ones when asked.
keyFacts: Human error is a top cause of data loss, e.g. deleting or overwriting files, or spilling drinks on kit
Protect with backups and file permissions, so mistakes can be undone and staff can't delete what they shouldn't
Training reduces mistakes, because staff learn safe ways to handle files and equipment

items.definition: Tricking people, not systems, into giving away information or access.
items.examples: A fake bank email asking you to "verify" your login.
items.examTip: It attacks the human. Phishing scenarios are common in exams.
keyFacts: Phishing: fake emails that look genuine, so users click links or enter passwords on fake sites
Vishing uses phone calls and smishing uses texts, so attackers reach people away from email filters
Pretexting: a made-up story to get information, e.g. posing as IT support to get a password
Baiting: infected USB sticks left lying around, so a curious finder plugs one in and installs malware
Defend with training, email filtering and MFA, so fewer attacks arrive and stolen passwords are useless alone

comparisonTable.title: Social Engineering Techniques Compared
rows: Email appearing to be from bank asking to 'verify' account
Email filtering; verify sender; never click unverified links
Email using victim's name and employer details to appear legitimate
Staff awareness training; verify requests through separate channel
Caller claiming to be IT support asking for password to 'fix an issue'
Never give passwords by phone; verify caller identity independently
Text claiming parcel delivery failed, asking to click link to rebook
Do not click links in unexpected texts; verify via official website
Fabricated scenario to justify information request
Attacker poses as HR to collect employee personal details for 'payroll update'
Verify identity via official channels before providing any information
Physical media left for victim to find and use
Infected USB drive left in company car park labelled 'Salary Data'
Policy against using unknown USB devices; security awareness training

items.definition: Floods, fires, earthquakes or lightning surges that destroy hardware and data.
items.examples: A flooded server room wiping out all on-site storage.
items.examTip: Link to off-site backups and disaster recovery plans.
keyFacts: Cannot be prevented, only prepared for, so organisations plan how to keep working after one
Off-site or cloud backups protect data, because a fire or flood at one site cannot destroy every copy
A disaster recovery plan sets out how to restore systems, so recovery is quick and downtime is short

subtopics.title: Types of Internal Threats to Data

items.definition: Staff visiting malicious, illegal or banned websites on work systems.
items.examples: A piracy site that silently installs malware.
items.examTip: Internal because it comes from an authorised user. Link to AUPs and web filtering.
keyFacts: Can bring in malware, because malicious sites may download harmful software onto work PCs
Legal liability for illegal content, because the organisation may be responsible for what is accessed on its systems
Controlled by web filtering and AUPs, so harmful sites are blocked and staff know the rules

items.definition: An employee sharing confidential data by mistake, which still counts as a data breach.
items.examples: Emailing customer data to the wrong person.
items.examTip: Still a GDPR breach even though it was accidental.
keyFacts: Serious breaches must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours, or the organisation can be fined
Causes include the wrong recipient, unencrypted files and lost devices, which are everyday slip-ups
Reduce with training and encryption, so mistakes are rarer and leaked files can't be read

items.definition: An insider deliberately copying, sharing or selling confidential data.
items.examples: A leaving employee copying the customer database to a USB stick.
items.examTip: The difference from accidental disclosure is intent.
keyFacts: Dangerous because insiders already have access, so they get past firewalls and passwords without hacking
Motives include money and grudges, e.g. selling customer data or getting revenge after being disciplined
Hard to spot among normal work, because copying files looks like the person doing their job
Reduce with least privilege and removing access promptly, so leavers and staff can't reach data they don't need

items.definition: USB sticks, laptops or personal phones used for work that can bring in malware or be lost.
items.examples: An unencrypted USB of patient records left on a train.
items.examTip: Two risks: malware coming in, and data lost if the device goes missing.
keyFacts: A lost unencrypted device is a GDPR breach, because anyone who finds it can read the personal data
Encrypt portable devices, so a lost or stolen laptop or USB stick is unreadable
Many organisations block USB ports, so malware can't come in and data can't be copied out
BYOD policies control personal devices, setting rules such as passcodes and remote wipe for work data

comparisonTable.title: Internal Threats Compared
rows: Visiting piracy site that installs malware
Emailing customer data to wrong address
Copying customer DB to USB before leaving
Losing unencrypted USB with patient data
Encryption, USB port controls, BYOD policy

items.definition: Data permanently lost, destroyed or made inaccessible.
items.examples: Ransomware with no backup; a flood destroying the only copy.
items.examTip: Link it to what follows: disruption, customers not served, lost revenue.
keyFacts: Without backups the loss may be permanent, so customer records or work may never be recovered
Organisation cannot operate normally, because orders, accounts and records may be missing
Prevent with off-site backups, so data can be restored even if the main site is destroyed

items.term: Financial Loss Due to Legal Action
items.definition: Fines from the ICO and lawsuits from people whose data was exposed.
items.examples: An ICO fine for failing to secure customer data.
items.examTip: Quote it: up to £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover, whichever is higher.
keyFacts: The ICO enforces UK data protection law, so it can investigate breaches and issue large fines
Breaches must be reported within 72 hours, and reporting late can increase the penalty
Extra costs (investigation, recovery, compensation) add to the fine and can cost more than it

items.term: Loss of Customers Due to Public Image
items.definition: A public breach damages trust, so customers leave and sales fall.
items.examples: A retailer losing customers to rivals after a card data breach.
items.examTip: Explain the chain: breach → bad publicity → lost trust → fewer customers → less revenue.
keyFacts: Trust is slow to rebuild, so customers may stay away long after the breach is fixed
Social media spreads bad news fast, so a breach becomes widely known within hours
Long-term losses can exceed the breach's direct cost, because lost customers mean lost future sales

subtopics.title: Techniques Used to Protect Data and Systems

items.definition: Settings on files and folders that control who can read, write, run or delete them.
items.examples: Only HR can open the payroll file; everyone else is read-only.
items.examTip: WHO can do WHAT with which files. Link to least privilege.
keyFacts: Read: view only, so staff can see information without being able to change it
Write: change or create, given only to people who need to update the files
Execute: run programs, so users can't run unknown software that could be malware
Set for individuals or groups, so a whole department can be given the right access in one step

items.definition: Levels of privilege that decide which systems and data each user can reach.
items.examples: Staff see their department's files; admins see everything.
items.examTip: Least privilege: each user gets only the access their job needs.
keyFacts: Guest → user → manager → administrator, with each level able to reach more systems and data
Based on job role, so staff only reach the data they need to do their work (least privilege)
Limits damage if an account is hacked, because the attacker only gets that user's level of access
Review when staff change roles or leave, so old access is removed before it can be misused

comparisonTable.title: File Permissions vs Access Levels
rows: What a user can do with a specific file/folder (read/write/execute/delete)
What systems, applications, and data a user can access at all
Broader — per role or user group
Only finance team can write to budget.xlsx
Only managers can log in to the HR management system
User account management / directory services (e.g. Active Directory)
Prevents unauthorised file modification or data leakage
Limits blast radius if account is compromised

items.definition: Regularly copying data to a separate place so it can be restored after loss.
items.examples: Nightly incremental backups plus a weekly full backup off-site.
items.examTip: Know full, incremental and differential, and why backups go off-site (fire, flood).
keyFacts: Full backup copies everything: slowest to make, but quickest to restore because only one set is needed
Incremental copies changes since the last backup: fast to make, but restoring needs every increment
Differential copies changes since the last full backup: restore needs only the full plus the latest differential
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site, so one fire, flood or failure can't destroy every copy
Test backups, because a backup that has never been restored may turn out to be corrupt or incomplete

comparisonTable.title: Backup Types Compared
rows: Only changes since last backup (full or incremental)
All changes since last full backup
Balance between storage and restore speed

items.definition: Passwords check who you are; MFA adds a second factor on top.
items.examples: A password plus a code from an authenticator app.
items.examTip: Name the factors: something you know, have and are.
keyFacts: Strong: 12+ characters, mixed types, not a word, so it takes far longer to guess or brute force
A stolen password alone is not enough with MFA, because the attacker also needs the second factor
Methods include an SMS code, app, hardware token or biometric, each something only the user has or is
Password managers stop reuse, so one leaked password doesn't unlock the user's other accounts

items.definition: Identifying people by unique body features such as fingerprint, face, iris or voice.
items.examples: Face unlock on a phone; fingerprint entry to an office.
items.examTip: "Something you are": cannot be forgotten, but cannot be changed if stolen.
keyFacts: Unique and cannot be shared, so access can't be passed on like a password or swipe card
Faster than typing a password, so staff log in quickly without writing passwords down
Cannot be reset if the data is stolen, because you can't change your fingerprint like a password
Privacy concerns under GDPR, because biometric data is sensitive and must be stored securely

items.definition: Physical measures that stop unauthorised people reaching IT equipment or data.
items.examples: Swipe cards for the server room; CCTV at entrances.
items.examTip: Physical security matters as much as cyber security.
keyFacts: Swipe cards and key fobs log who enters, so access is limited and there is a record if something goes wrong
Biometric locks on secure rooms, so only authorised people can reach servers or sensitive data
CCTV and guards deter intruders, and footage gives evidence if equipment is stolen
Clear desk policy, so papers and unlocked screens can't be read or photographed by visitors

items.definition: Electronic ID issued by a Certificate Authority that proves a website is genuine and enables encryption.
items.examples: The padlock icon in a browser.
items.examTip: Certificate = proof of identity + enables encryption. Expired ones trigger warnings.
keyFacts: Issued by a trusted Certificate Authority, which checks the owner's identity first
Contains the owner's public key and an expiry date, so browsers can encrypt traffic and reject old certificates
Stops attackers impersonating a site, because a fake site cannot show a valid certificate for that domain

subtopics.title: Features and Functions of Antivirus Software

items.definition: Software that finds, quarantines and removes malware using signatures and behaviour checks.
items.examples: Windows Defender blocking a downloaded trojan.
items.examTip: Must be updated. Heuristics catch new, unknown threats.
keyFacts: Signatures match known malware, so recognised threats are detected reliably
Heuristics spot suspicious behaviour, so new malware with no signature yet can still be caught
Real-time scanning checks files as they open or download, so threats are stopped before they run
Quarantine isolates infected files, so they can't spread while the user decides what to do
Useless against new threats without updates, because its signature list goes out of date

items.definition: Monitors traffic in and out of a network and blocks it according to rules.
items.examples: Blocking incoming traffic on ports the business doesn't use.
items.examTip: Describe it: monitors traffic, applies rules, forms a barrier between networks.
keyFacts: Checks addresses and ports against rules, so only permitted traffic gets in or out
Can block sites, apps and IP ranges, so known malicious sources can't reach the network
Hardware firewall protects the whole network, guarding every device behind it at once
Software firewall protects one device, so a laptop stays protected on other networks too
Cannot stop insider threats, because staff are already inside the network the firewall guards

comparisonTable.title: Hardware Firewall vs Software Firewall
rows: Network perimeter — between internet and internal network
Only the device it is installed on
None on individual devices — runs on dedicated hardware
Uses some CPU and RAM on the host device
Higher upfront cost for dedicated appliance
Often free (built into OS) or low-cost subscription
Centralised — IT team manages rules for all devices
Decentralised — each device has its own settings
Does not protect against threats originating inside the network
Only protects one device; user may disable it
Individual users; supplementary layer on specific devices

subtopics.title: Features and Functions of Encryption Methods

items.term: Encryption of Stored Data (Data at Rest)
items.definition: Encrypting stored data so a stolen device or drive cannot be read.
items.examples: BitLocker on a laptop; an encrypted customer database.
items.examTip: If the key is lost, the data is lost too.
keyFacts: Full disk encryption (e.g. BitLocker) encrypts the whole drive, so nothing on it is readable without the key
Protects stolen laptops, USBs and backups, so a theft does not become a data breach
Keep the key separate and secure, because anyone with the key can decrypt the data

items.term: Encryption of Data During Transmission (Data in Transit)
items.definition: Encrypting data as it travels so it cannot be read if intercepted.
items.examples: VPN traffic; end-to-end encrypted WhatsApp messages.
items.examTip: Key methods: TLS (HTTPS, email) and VPNs.
keyFacts: End-to-end: only sender and recipient can read it, so not even the service provider can see messages
Symmetric uses one shared key, so it is fast, but the key must be shared safely first
Asymmetric: the public key encrypts and the private key decrypts, so no secret key needs sharing
Public Wi-Fi is risky without it, because others on the network can intercept unencrypted traffic

items.definition: HTTP secured with TLS: encrypts traffic between browser and server and proves the server is genuine.
items.examples: Online banking and checkout pages.
items.examTip: HTTPS gives encryption, integrity and authentication.
keyFacts: Padlock means a valid certificate, so users can check the connection is encrypted before entering details
Certificate proves the server's identity, so users know they're on the genuine site, not a fake
Over plain HTTP, logins can be sniffed, because usernames and passwords travel as readable text

comparisonTable.title: Encryption Contexts Compared
rows: Data being sent across a network
Web traffic between browser and server
While data is stored / device is offline
OS/disk encryption software; DBA for databases
